onPurposeCareersNewsletter.bodyPreview:
Hi there,

In today's issue, I'm writing about the use of AI bots to apply for you and why that might be working against you.

* **Stop using AI bots to apply for you**

* **New remote social impact jobs**

-Navid
Do good work. Get paid well.

———————————————————————————

# **Stop using AI bots to apply for you. It's not helping your case.**

I spoke with a recruiter recently on a podcast to dispel myths from across the hiring table. One of the things we uncovered was AI in the application process. The obvious topic we've all seen before: can everyone tell I'm using AI on my resume and cover letter? The answer is uh, yES.

The other AI flag, popping up more recently, is when candidates pay for AI bots to apply on their behalf. This one's particularly easy to spot, and it might be working against you.

When bots apply for you (and hundreds of other applicants), those applications all land at the same time using the same language. Systems will often alert employers about suspicious activity from AI bots, and your application may not even get considered.

So what actually works?

Quality beats quantity here. My take: 5-10 thoughtful, tailored applications a week will get you further than 100 bot-blasted ones.

That doesn't mean AI is off limits. Used right, it can be an important tool to help you make sure you're calling out the details the job is seeking, as well as a prep tool.

Use it to brainstorm talking points, stress-test your answers, or organize your thoughts before you write. The output still needs to sound like you, because it's you who has to sit in that interview and back it up.

The bots may move fast, but you can move smarter.
